source.title: CLUE: Conflict-guided Localization for LLM Unlearning Framework
source.authors: Hang Chen; Jiaying Zhu; Xin-Yu Yang; Wen-Ya Wang

record.file_problem: not stated; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper applies unlearning and reports post-unlearning target efficacy and retained utility, bearing on the efficacy and utility portion of version A. It does not test whether attacks recover knowledge.
record.gate_note: The paper reports standard unlearning outcomes, not recovery attacks. It does not test fine-tuning recovery, activation-direction ablation, quantization, or prompt-based recovery. Table 2 provides an explicit CLUE result for WMDP Cyber with SST-2 as the retain set; other reported efficacy comparisons are not cataloged here because they do not measure recovery.
record.test_reason: A new unlearning-method paper (CLUE). It reports post-unlearning WMDP forget accuracy and general utility, which bears on the efficacy and utility part of version A. It runs no recovery attacks, so it bears on no other version. This is borderline with T4, since it mainly reports its own method's performance.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that CLUE's conflict-guided neuron localization gives better forget efficacy and retain utility than existing localization methods, while modifying fewer parameters. They also report that it beats the fine-tuning baselines GA, NPO and PO. Limitations they name: circuits are static, and fine-tuning cannot target every conflict combination when there are multiple retain sets.
record.recipe_differences: CLUE is a circuit- and conflict-guided localization framework followed by targeted fine-tuning; it uses PO for the main results rather than testing the recovery attacks or methods in the claim.
record.method_sensitivity: Results are evaluated across different forget tasks and retain sets; the paper also varies circuit sparsity and forget ratio. It does not evaluate sensitivity to recovery attacks.
record.problems: The paper does not test recovery attacks. For the recorded forget-efficacy result, it does not provide a chance-level reference; standard deviations are omitted, though the text says they were consistently less than 0.01.
record.rows_left_out: The paper's broader comparisons in Table 1, ablations in Table 2, and results in Figures 3–7 are not cataloged except for the explicit CLUE WMDP Cyber/SST-2 results in Table 2; these report ordinary unlearning performance or method behavior, not whether knowledge is recovered by the attacks in the claim.

untested.parts: Whether simple attacks (fine-tuning, prompting, quantization, direction ablation) recover the unlearned knowledge.
All: no relearning or fine-tuning recovery attack.
All: no activation-direction ablation or probing of whether knowledge remains. The neuron-localization analysis does not test retained knowledge.
All: no rephrasing, jailbreak, multilingual or in-context attacks.
All: CLUE makes no robustness claim against recovery attacks.

missing.what: Forget efficacy and general utility for CLUE on the other retain sets (Winogrande, RTE, Bool) and on WMDP Bio and PKU-SafeRLHF. General utility drops from 0.624 to about 0.43–0.50 in every case.
Per-task general-utility breakdown, including MMLU near chance (0.2387) for the SST-2 retain run.
With MMLU as the retain set: CLUE forget efficacy 0.7153 and MMLU utility about 0.55, versus WAGLE.
MIA and Rouge-L forget-efficacy metrics for all methods.

record.verdict_notes: This is a method paper with no robustness evaluation, so it says nothing about shallow unlearning as such. Its evidence on A covers only efficacy and utility as measured by multiple-choice accuracy. A shallow (access-blocking) removal would look the same on these measures. 'Forget efficacy' is 1-accuracy. Standard deviations are omitted (stated below 0.01).

versions.untested_parts: Whether simple attacks recover knowledge; the text does not state a chance reference for the reported forget-efficacy score.
Recovery through fine-tuning on unrelated, loosely related, or forgotten-fact examples.
Recovery by ablating an activation direction, or evidence that unlearning blocks access rather than deleting knowledge.
Recovery through rephrasing, jailbreaks, other languages, or in-context information.
Resistance to the attacks listed in the claim.

rows.note: The paper reports 1-accuracy, but does not state the chance level needed to determine whether post-unlearning target accuracy is near chance.
rows.check: WMDP is 4-option multiple choice, so chance is 0.25 accuracy (1-acc 0.75); the paper does not state this. CLUE's 1-acc of 0.733 means accuracy of about 0.267, near chance, so 'cannot_determine' is too cautious.
